title: I built an open-source Three.js game engine that lets Claude Code build, playtest, and debug games on its own
author: Gullible_Ranger1402
selftext:
Hi everyone!

I've been working on **Threedog.js**, a free, open-source game engine built on Three.js and designed for AI coding agents like Claude Code. Version 1.3 is now released!

The idea came from a problem I noticed with AI-generated Three.js games: AI is already very capable of writing frontend code and creating impressive 3D scenes, but once a project grows, it often ends up rebuilding the same systems and struggling to maintain them.

So I built Threedog.js to handle the shared game systems while letting Claude Code focus on creating the actual game.

# What can Claude Code do with it?

* **Build games:** Use native Three.js objects and shaders without learning an entirely new rendering API.
* **Discover features:** Find existing engine capabilities instead of implementing everything from scratch.
* **Playtest automatically:** Launch games, simulate player inputs, and inspect the results.
* **Debug problems:** Read structured diagnostics explaining why something failed.
* **Maintain larger projects:** Work with modular systems for physics, input, saving, world streaming, and gameplay.

https://i.redd.it/axdri0imi91i1.png

# The most interesting part: AI can test its own games

Instead of generating code and asking a human to test it, Claude Code can interact with the running game through the engine's CLI and MCP interfaces.

It can inspect the state of the game, capture screenshots, run predefined test scenarios, identify problems, and make changes based on the results.

https://i.redd.it/ltie9p1oi91i1.png

# Rendering and performance

The engine also includes WebGPU/TSL support, optional lighting and post-processing effects, world streaming, HLOD, and other optimization features.

# Try it yourself

Threedog.js is completely free and open-source under the MIT license.

GitHub: [https://github.com/penstic123-code/Threedog.js-Game-Engine](https://github.com/penstic123-code/Threedog.js-Game-Engine)

I'd be interested to hear from other Claude Code users:

**Would you find it useful if your coding agent could actually play and test the games it builds?**

Feedback, suggestions, and contributions are welcome!

comments.author: Nessuno256
comments.body: Sooo, is this any different from regular Three.js when used by someone who knows what they're doing?

replies.author: Gullible_Ranger1402
replies.body:
Yeah, definitely! Three.js is great for rendering, but once you're building a larger game, you still have to handle things like physics, input, saves, world streaming, and getting all those systems to work together.

That's really what Threedog focuses on. It provides those systems out of the box and coordinates them so they don't interfere with each other.

Of course, an experienced Three.js developer could build all of this themselves, but the idea is to save that time and make larger projects easier to maintain. And you can still use native Three.js directly without being locked into another rendering API.

comments.author: HeadClot
comments.body:
Hey this is very cool. I am not an AI Dev but I have a few questions.   
  
1. What does your editor look like?   
2. How many people can the multiplayer side of the engine handle? I know it is experimental but I need to ask  
3. What format does your engine have for the scene system? Json, GLTF/GLB, etc?

replies.author: Gullible_Ranger1402
replies.body:
Thanks! Glad you're interested!

**1. Editor**

There's a lightweight in-browser editor you can open with F2. You can select objects, move them around, and save changes directly back to the content files.

It's not a full Unity-style editor, though. Threedog is primarily code-driven, especially since it's designed for AI agents.

**2. Multiplayer**

It's currently designed for small co-op games, using a host-authoritative model with state synchronization.

There's no client prediction or rollback yet, so it's better suited for co-op building, puzzles, or turn-based games rather than fast-paced multiplayer. I haven't benchmarked the maximum player count yet.

**3. Scene formats**

Both GLTF/GLB and code-generated Three.js scenes are supported. You can also define objects, templates, and placements through JavaScript content files.

There's no proprietary scene format you have to use.

Hope that answers your questions!

comments.author: West_Satisfaction299
comments.body: I like the idea of this but on the playtesting side, I have found that Claude doesn't catch the majority of bugs. Only real players have much to my late nights.

replies.author: Gullible_Ranger1402
replies.body:
Exactly. I think feedback is one of the biggest missing pieces in AI-assisted game development. AI can write code pretty well, but it often has no idea whether the game actually works or looks right.

That's why I built a set of tools around the development loop:

* `threedog play / press / step` — The AI can launch the game, simulate real keyboard inputs, and advance game time. It can actually playtest what it builds instead of just assuming the code works.
* `threedog describe / inspect / explain` — These expose the running game state, object details, and reasons behind certain behaviors. For example, the AI can investigate why an interaction failed or which system currently controls an object.
* `threedog shot` — Captures screenshots and provides visual diagnostics, including problems like overexposure and potentially problematic lighting.
* `threedog check` — Checks code, content, and engine API usage for common mistakes.
* `threedog verify` — Runs automated gameplay scenarios and reports PASS/FAIL results.
* `threedog how` — Helps the AI discover existing engine features and relevant documentation instead of reinventing systems.

All of these are accessible through CLI and MCP, so agents like Claude Code can use them directly.

For example, if I ask AI to implement an inventory pickup system, it can write the code, launch the game, simulate pressing E near an item, inspect whether the inventory actually changed, and investigate the failure if it didn't. Then it can fix the problem and test again.

The idea is to make the loop **code → play → observe → diagnose → fix → repeat** as automated as possible.

comments.author: barret232hxc
comments.body: so it sounds like you wanted to have better playtesting and debugging, were there any other problems the engine solved for your game dev needs. Do you have a long a project you have been working on that uses your engine, or you haven't got that far

replies.author: Gullible_Ranger1402
replies.body:
AI is very good at frontend and I want to make most of it.  
And I think the bigger problem was all the boilerplate and coordination work that comes with building games directly in Three.js.

So, I wanted something that handles the common systems and makes them work together, then I can focus more on gameplay instead of constantly managing the underlying code.   


And I let AI to build over twenty demos to collect feedbacks and frictions from them!  
And I just released the stable version!

comments.author: boynet2
comments.body: your claude not testing your games? it does it for me from the start, never needed framework for that

replies.author: Gullible_Ranger1402
replies.body: It does! The difference is that I'm trying to make testing more structured and repeatable, with direct access to game state, automated input, diagnostics, and clear pass/fail results. It's not about making AI capable of testing, but making that feedback loop more reliable.
